Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
The event happened because of the way I acted
I acted in ways that go against who I am

vignette:
Sofia was twenty-five when the relationship turned, though she would later tell herself she should have seen it coming. Her boyfriend Carlos had always been quick to anger-slamming cabinet doors, muttering under his breath-but the first time he shoved her, she made excuses. She had been late coming home from the animation studio, he had been drinking, she had talked back. Over the next year, the shoves became slaps, the slaps became closed-fist blows to her ribs and arms, always in places she could hide with long sleeves or a shrug. The worst night happened after she told him she was thinking of leaving. He pinned her against the bathroom wall by her throat, his forearm pressed across her collarbone, and when she tried to push him away he grabbed her wrist and twisted until she heard something pop. She did not scream because she was certain that if she made a sound he would kill her. That was the night she finally left, but the leaving did not undo what had already lodged itself inside her.

Now, two years later, Sofia still cannot shake the belief that she has become someone else entirely-someone smaller, more frightened, untrustworthy to herself. She replays the moment she froze during that final assault, the way her body went limp instead of fighting, and she is convinced that she failed a fundamental test of character. She had always thought of herself as strong, as someone who would never tolerate being hurt. But she did tolerate it, month after month, and the memory of those choices-the arguments she started, the apologies she made, the nights she stayed-feels like a stain she cannot wash out. She tells herself that a decent person would have walked away the first time. Instead, she acted in ways that contradict everything she believed about loyalty, about standing up for herself, about love. The weight of that contradiction sits in her chest like a bruise that never heals.

Sofia works from home now, animating characters for a children's series about a cheerful young fox. The studio gives her freelance contracts, and she has stopped going to the office altogether. She cannot bear the walk past the coffee shop where Carlos used to meet her after work, the way it smells like his cologne. More than that, she cannot bear the unpredictability of other people's bodies-the casual touch of a colleague's hand on her shoulder, a door slamming in the hallway, a man raising his voice to order lunch. Each one sends her heart into her throat. In the safety of her apartment, she curates her world carefully: no romantic comedies, no scenes of arguments, no dates. She tells herself it is just easier. When her supervisor asked her to animate a brief scuffle between the fox and a rival character, Sofia spent three days avoiding the assignment before finally requesting a different sequence, citing creative differences. She did not explain the real reason-that the sight of a hand raised in anger on her screen made her breath catch, her vision blur, and the memory of Carlos's knuckles come flooding back.

The consequences have crept up on her. She used to call her sister weekly; now she keeps calls short and vague, afraid of being asked why she is still single, whether she is dating, what happened to that nice guy from animation school. Her sister has stopped asking. Sofia has stopped noticing how small her world has become. She works, she sleeps, she avoids. The only place she feels somewhat safe is inside the fox's tidy little world, where no one ever really hurts anyone.

Last month, during a routine video call with a producer, the man cleared his throat sharply-a sound exactly like the one Carlos made before losing his temper. Sofia's screen went black as she dropped her laptop; she spent the next hour shaking on her bathroom floor, certain she was back in that apartment, pinned against the wall, about to die. After that, she called a therapist. She is terrified that she will never be the person she used to be, that she has been permanently reshaped into someone broken beyond repair. But she is also, somewhere underneath the fear, exhausted by the constant vigilance. She wants to stop feeling like a stranger inside her own life. She wants to believe she deserves to feel safe again.
